title: Trump Administration Moves to Scrap H-1B 60-Day Grace Period After Job Loss
excerpt: A DHS proposal published September 10 would require H-1B and other temporary workers to leave the U.S. as soon as employment ends - with Indian professionals the most exposed.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security published a proposed rule on September 10, 2026 that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for laid-off H-1B and other temporary workers.
  • The protection, in place since 2017, lets workers find a new sponsor, change immigration status, or wind up their affairs after a job ends.
  • Under the proposal, affected workers would have to leave the United States as soon as their employment ends; a two-month public comment period now opens before any final rule.
  • Indian nationals — about 71 percent of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal 2024 — would bear the brunt of any final rule.

Grace Period on the Chopping Block

The Trump administration has proposed eliminating a 60-day grace period that allows certain immigrants, including skilled workers on H-1B visas, to stay in the United States and find a new sponsor after losing their job, according to a government notice posted Thursday. Under the planned rule change, published in the Federal Register by the Department of Homeland Security, those with H-1B and certain other temporary work visas would have to leave the country as soon as their employment ends — a potential blow to top American tech companies that rely heavily on foreign workers.

https://x.com/adaderana/status/2098096331936207021

Titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period" (regulatory number 1615-AD22), the proposal cleared White House review at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on August 27 and is now open for public comment, Bloomberg Law and IANS reported.

Context & Background

The grace period has been in place since 2017 under Obama-era regulations. It allows eligible workers up to 60 consecutive days after employment ends — or until their authorized stay expires, whichever is shorter — to find another employer willing to sponsor them, seek a change of immigration status, or prepare to leave the United States. The window covers H-1B specialty occupation workers as well as L-1 intracompany transferees, O-1 visa holders of extraordinary ability, TN professionals, E-1 and E-2 visa holders, H-1B1 workers from Singapore and Chile, and E-3 specialty workers from Australia.

The proposal is the latest in a series of Trump administration measures reshaping legal immigration since January 2025, including higher visa fees for skilled workers, a pause on immigrant visa appointments at U.S. missions worldwide, a proposed $103,265 fee for new H-1B hires reported this week, and the final rule replacing "duration of status" admissions for F-1 students effective September 15.

DHS argues the change would reduce administrative burdens and restore a direct link between a foreign worker's status and the employment that was its basis. Companies affected could see some disruption, the proposal said, but the jobs could go to American workers instead. "DHS presumes that they will either offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers or go through the I-129 petition process depending on their workforce requirement," the notice said.

Impact & Analysis

For employers, the timeline compression would be severe. Layoffs of visa-holding staff would have to be managed against an immediate departure clock rather than a two-month runway.

"[The move] would sharply compress the timeline HR teams have to manage layoffs and offboarding for foreign national employees."

— Lawyers for Berardi Immigration Law, via Reuters

The workers' side is starker. A laid-off H-1B holder currently has up to 60 days to land a new sponsor or change status — time that also covers the practical realities of an uprooted life, from selling a home to pulling children out of school, as Reuters noted. Under the proposal, that cushion disappears: the end of the job is effectively the end of lawful stay.

Top H-1B sponsors named by Reuters include consultancy firms Deloitte, PwC and Ernst & Young, along with outsourcing giants Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCL Tech and LTIMindtree — meaning the rule would ripple through the exact firms where Indian professionals are concentrated.

Diaspora Angle

This proposal lands squarely on the Indian diaspora. Indian nationals accounted for about 71 percent of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal 2024, according to figures cited by Mint. A layoff in a volatile tech market would no longer mean two months to find a new sponsor — it would mean an abrupt departure order for the worker and their family.

What's Next

None of this is final yet. The proposal now enters a 60-day public comment period, and DHS must consider the comments before issuing any final rule — which could move forward, be modified, delayed, or withdrawn. Immigration attorneys stress that the existing 60-day grace period remains in force and workers should not assume it has been canceled.

What H-1B holders can do now: keep immigration documents and status timelines current, build a contingency plan for a job loss — including identifying potential sponsors in advance — and consult an immigration lawyer before acting on the proposal.
nri_angle: Indian nationals were about 71 percent of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal 2024, so eliminating the grace period would turn any tech layoff into an immediate departure order for Indian workers and their families.
